1:5.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

provenance.route: John 21:25 (with John 20:30) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “could not contain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 21:25 and John 20:30, the two closing statements of the Fourth Gospel. Neither phrase is reproduced here. “hundredth part” also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is a sum of money and has nothing to do with writing; see the exclusion register.
provenance.alternative: The inexpressibility topos is ancient and near-universal, and the Book of Mormon has its own settled formula for it (“a hundredth part”, already at Jacob 3:13), so this verse may be quoting nothing but itself.
provenance.significance: What makes the pairing worth recording is not the sentiment but the genre. Words of Mormon is a compiler's colophon: a named redactor breaks frame to explain which records he had, which he chose, and why the rest is omitted. The KJV has one other passage that does exactly this — John 20:30-31 and 21:25, where a named witness says that much was done which is not written in this book, and that what is written was selected for the reader's benefit. Mormon's ‘I chose these things’ (1:5) and ‘that perhaps some day it may profit them’ (1:2) are the two halves of John's colophon in reverse order.

1:5.note: ‘I cannot write a hundredth part of the things of my people.’ Recorded as a risk, not as a demonstration: there is no shared wording at all. The case rests entirely on form — this is a redactor's colophon, and the KJV supplies exactly one model for a redactor's colophon, which the Book of Mormon's own colophons resemble in shape and function. The 1830 reads ‘a hundredth part’ where 1920 reads ‘the hundredth part’; the definite article moves the phrase toward Nehemiah 5:11's, which is the one place the KJV has it, and away from what the sentence means.
1:5.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives the comparison. The topos requires no source, the Book of Mormon has used the formula before Mormon writes, and a reader who declines this row loses nothing from the chapter's argument.

1:7.text: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 29:29 + Acts 15:18 → KJV → 1 Nephi 9:5-6 → Words of Mormon 1:7
provenance.other: “knoweth all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:20, where it is a consolation for a condemning heart and not a statement about foreknowledge; the sense here is Acts 15:18's, and 1 John 3:20 is filed in the exclusion register. “a wise purpose” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses — it is the Book of Mormon's own phrase, coined at 1 Nephi 9:5.
provenance.significance: Mormon is not reaching past Nephi to the Bible; he is reaching to Nephi. 1 Nephi 9:5-6 set the two propositions side by side in this order — the plates are made for a purpose their maker does not know, and the Lord knows all things — and Words of Mormon 1:7 reproduces the pair, in that order, at the moment when the small plates whose purpose Nephi did not know are being handed on to the compiler who still does not know it. The Book of Mormon is here quoting its own account of the very object it is discussing. Recover the biblical layer and the point sharpens further: Acts 15:18 is spoken at the council that admits Gentiles on new terms, justified by the claim that God knew all along, and the small plates are the book's own instance of a provision whose reason appears only from the other end.

1:7.note: ‘And I do this for a wise purpose … And now, I do not know all things; but the Lord knoweth all things which is to come.’ This is 1 Nephi 9:5-6 in miniature, with the biblical sources reaching Mormon through Nephi rather than directly: Deuteronomy 29:29's division of knowledge between God and a scribe, and Acts 15:18's assertion that God has known his own works from the beginning. Nothing here is a fresh borrowing; the proximate model is the Book of Mormon's earlier text, which is why the mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM even though the ultimate source at the second half of the sentence is a New Testament verse. Note the 1830 reading ‘all things which is to come’, corrected to ‘are’ in 1920 — the first edition preserves the singular concord that the later text tidied away.

1:7.text: For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.

provenance.other: “worketh in” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, of which Philippians 2:13 is the only one with God as subject, a person as object, and an infinitive of doing attached. Colossians 1:29's ‘which worketh in me mightily’ supplies the first-person object but not the willing and doing.
provenance.significance: Philippians 2:13 is the KJV's formula for divine agency inside a human agent who is nevertheless acting: it stands immediately after ‘work out your own salvation with fear and trembling’, and its force is that the working is God's and the working out is yours. Mormon needs precisely that construction. He has just said that he does not know why he is including these plates, only that something whispers it; the sentence that follows has to make an unexplained editorial decision into an obedient one without claiming knowledge, and Paul's sentence is the one in the KJV that does that job.

1:7.note: ‘Wherefore, he worketh in me to do according to his will.’ Three of the four elements of Philippians 2:13 are here and in Paul's order — God as the one working, a person worked in, and an infinitive ‘to do’ — with ‘according to his will’ standing where Paul has ‘of his good pleasure’. The substitution is itself worth noting, since ‘his good pleasure’ would have been the more distinctive borrowing and the Book of Mormon declines it; what it takes is the syntax of the clause, not its ornament. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion accordingly.

1:8.text: And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.

provenance.other: “delightsome” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. It is not a common English word in 1611 or in 1830, and the Book of Mormon uses it repeatedly and only of a restored people.
provenance.significance: Malachi 3:12 is the promise attached to the tithe: bring the whole tithe, and the nations will call you blessed, for you will be a delightsome land. Mormon's prayer changes the noun — a delightsome people, not a delightsome land — and in doing so moves the promise off the territory his people have just lost and onto the people themselves. He is writing at the point where the land is forfeit and the nation nearly extinct; the one KJV word for restored favour is available to him only if it can be detached from real estate, and he detaches it. The rest of Malachi 3 is the day of refining that the Book of Mormon's last chapters assume.

1:8.note: ‘That they may once again be a delightsome people.’ The adjective is a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon's use of it is unmistakably Malachi's covenant-restoration sense rather than any ordinary English one. The visible change is land to people, which is the whole burden of Mormon's prayer: the brethren he prays for have no land to be called blessed in. Well below a quotation's length — one word plus its grammatical frame — but a one-word borrowing from a one-verse source is stronger evidence than a long run of common wording.

1:11.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “judged out of those things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The construction ‘judged out of’ a written record is Revelation 20:12's alone; no Old Testament judgment scene has it, and Daniel 7:10's ‘the books were opened’ stops short of saying that the judgment is drawn from their contents.
provenance.significance: This is the sentence where the colophon turns into an eschatological claim about itself. Mormon prays that the plates be preserved, and the reason he gives for expecting the prayer to be answered is that his people will be judged out of what is written on them — which is Revelation 20:12's clause with the plates substituted for the opened books of the last judgment. The effect is to place the object in the reader's hands inside the assize scene: the record is not merely a witness to the judgment, it is one of the books. Compare the same move at the end of Moroni, where the writer expects to meet his reader at the bar of God.

1:11.note: ‘There are great things written upon them, out of which my people and their brethren shall be judged at the great and last day, according to the word of God which is written.’ Revelation 20:12's distinctive clause is ‘the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works’, and Words of Mormon has its three moving parts in Revelation's order: judged, out of what is written, according to a standard. The Book of Mormon substitutes ‘according to the word of God which is written’ for ‘according to their works’, which shifts the criterion from deeds to text and is consistent with a sentence whose subject is a record. ‘Great and last day’ is the Book of Mormon's own formula and occurs in no KJV verse.

1:11.text: Now I pray to God that ye do no evil; not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates.

provenance.other: “pray to God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Every other instance of the construction in the KJV is ‘pray unto God’, ‘pray unto the LORD’, or ‘pray for’; the preposition ‘to’ with ‘God’ after ‘pray’ is 2 Corinthians 13:7's alone.
provenance.significance: The finding is not this verse by itself but the pair. Words of Mormon 1:11 has the KJV singleton “pray to God”, from 2 Corinthians 13:7; Words of Mormon 1:17 has the KJV singleton “use sharpness”, from 2 Corinthians 13:10, three verses further down the same page; and 1:9's ‘according to the knowledge and the understanding which God hath given me’ answers to 13:10's ‘according to the power which the Lord hath given me’. Two singletons and a third phrase from a six-verse span of one Pauline passage is the pattern already recorded at 1 Nephi 4:2 with Hebrews 11 — a chapter of the Bible being worked through in order rather than quoted at a point. What Paul is doing across 2 Corinthians 13:7-10 is exactly what Mormon is doing here: an absent writer explaining, in the last paragraph of a letter, why he writes as he does and what he prays will come of it.

1:11.note: ‘And I, Mormon, pray to God that they may be preserved.’ Taken alone the phrase would be too short to argue from, however rare; what recommends it is that the same chapter reaches into the same four verses of 2 Corinthians twice more, once for a second KJV singleton (see 1:17) and once for the ‘according to … which the Lord hath given me’ construction at 1:9. Confidence is held at moderate because a writer could arrive at ‘pray to God’ without a source; the recurrence, not the phrase, is the evidence.

1:13.text: With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

provenance.other: “arm of flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon does not reproduce the phrase here; what it reproduces is the antithesis the phrase belongs to.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 32:7-8 is Hezekiah's speech to his captains as Sennacherib's army comes up: the invader has an arm of flesh, we have the LORD to fight our battles. Words of Mormon 1:13-14 sets a king before an invading army and gives the same two terms in the same order across the verse break — the strength of his own arm in 1:13, the strength of the Lord in 1:14 — with the second superseding the first. Whether the writer had Hezekiah in view or not, the Book of Mormon's one detailed sentence about Benjamin as a war leader is built on the KJV's one formal statement that a king's own arm is the wrong thing to trust.

1:13.note: ‘He did fight with the strength of his own arm, with the sword of Laban; and in the strength of the Lord they did contend against their enemies.’ The verbal contact is slight and the structural contact is exact: an arm of flesh, then the LORD who fights our battles. Note that the Book of Mormon lets the king keep his own arm rather than rebuking it, which is a real departure from Hezekiah's speech and the reason this is filed as an echo rather than an allusion. The sword of Laban in the same clause is the book's own relic, first taken at 1 Nephi 4, and is not biblical.
1:13.whyNot: ‘Strength of his own arm’ is not 2 Chronicles 32:8's wording, and a battle narrative that credits the Lord for the victory needs no particular source; the argument is entirely from the shape of the antithesis.

1:14.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.route: Psalm 71:16 (with Micah 5:4) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Neither is a battle report: the first is an old man's vow to keep going, the second is the shepherd-ruler from Bethlehem standing and feeding his flock.
provenance.significance: Both KJV occurrences of the phrase describe a person sustained rather than an army winning, and Micah 5:4's is the one the Book of Mormon's readers would recognise — the ruler who shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD, in a chapter the New Testament attaches to Christ's birth. Applying it to King Benjamin's campaign gives the war a royal-messianic colouring that the surrounding sentences do not otherwise carry, and it prepares for 1:17-18, where the same king is a holy man reigning in righteousness rather than a general.

1:14.note: ‘And in the strength of the Lord they did contend against their enemies.’ The phrase is rare and the Book of Mormon has it verbatim; what it does not have is either source's setting, which is why this is an allusion at moderate rather than a quotation. The pairing with 1:13's ‘strength of his own arm’ is the argument for taking it as a deliberate contrast rather than a stock phrase.

1:15.text: For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.

provenance.route: Matthew 24:24 or Mark 13:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “false Christs” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22, which are the same saying in the two synoptic apocalypses. `tools/mediation-check.py` returns no decisive divergence between them at any point Words of Mormon reproduces: the Book of Mormon has neither Matthew's ‘there shall arise’ nor Mark's ‘shall rise’, and takes none of the signs-and-wonders material that follows in either. The source is one of the two and the text cannot say which.
provenance.significance: The pair ‘false Christs … false prophets’ exists in the KJV only inside the Olivet discourse, as a sign of the end. Words of Mormon puts it in the past tense and in a civil register — they had been, their mouths had been shut, they were punished according to their crimes — so an eschatological warning becomes a summary of law enforcement under a good king. The compression is the interesting part: what Jesus predicts as the mark of the last days is here a solved administrative problem, two verses before Benjamin establishes peace.

1:15.note: ‘After there had been false Christs, and their mouths had been shut, and they punished according to their crimes.’ ‘False Christs’ carries the whole link and carries it well, since the KJV has it in two verses only and they are one saying; 1:16 then supplies the second half of that saying, ‘false prophets’, before moving to a different New Testament source. The chief oddity is chronological rather than verbal, and it is the kind of thing this catalogue exists to record: a Nephite king some hundred and thirty years before the nativity is putting down false Christs, in the phrase Matthew and Mark coin for the impostors of the last days.

1:16.text: But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.

provenance.other: “false teachers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘False prophets’ occurs in seven, but 2 Peter 2:1 is the only verse in the Bible that holds false prophets, false teachers and ‘among the people’ in a single sentence, and Words of Mormon 1:16 holds all three in that order. ‘False preachers’ is in no KJV verse; the Book of Mormon has expanded the doublet into a triplet with a word of its own.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 2:1 is a sentence about historical repetition — there were false prophets then, as there will be false teachers now — and the Book of Mormon is at this moment doing exactly what the sentence describes, transposing the phenomenon into a further period. Mormon writes the verse from the far side of the analogy: for him the apostolic ‘shall be’ has become another ‘there had been’, in a nation Peter never had in view. The verse in Peter goes on to the destruction those teachers bring on themselves; Words of Mormon supplies it as ‘punished according to their crimes’, which is the civil version of the same clause.

1:16.note: ‘After there had been false prophets, and false preachers and teachers among the people.’ Two KJV terms and their prepositional phrase, in 2 Peter's own order, with one non-biblical term interpolated between them. The interpolation is what makes the borrowing visible rather than obscuring it: had the Book of Mormon written ‘false prophets and false teachers’ the phrase could be a commonplace, but the awkward ‘false preachers and teachers’ reads like a source being stretched to cover a third office. Falls well below a quotation's length and is catalogued as an allusion.

1:17.text: Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.

provenance.other: “use sharpness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘sharpness’ itself occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Three verses earlier in the same passage, “pray to God” is also a KJV singleton and is borrowed at Words of Mormon 1:11; 1:9's ‘according to the knowledge and the understanding which God hath given me’ answers to 13:10's ‘according to the power which the Lord hath given me’.
provenance.significance: Recovering the context turns the sentence over. Paul uses sharpness ‘according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction’ — the sharpness is licensed by authority and limited by its purpose. Words of Mormon 1:17 has the licence in the immediately preceding clause: the holy men speak ‘with power and with authority’, and therefore ‘did use much sharpness’. Both halves of Paul's sentence are present, in Paul's order, with the causal link intact and the biblical restraint — to edification and not to destruction — left unstated. That silence is the finding: the Book of Mormon takes Paul's warrant for severity and drops his limit on it, then shows the severity working, since peace is established by 1:18.

1:17.note: ‘They did speak the word of God, with power and with authority; and they did use much sharpness, because of the stiffneckedness of the people.’ A KJV singleton reproduced with its governing verb, from a verse whose remaining clause supplies the authority-language of the sentence before it. What makes this the chapter's strongest row is not the phrase alone but its neighbourhood: two KJV singletons from a four-verse span of 2 Corinthians 13 appear in this chapter, at 1:11 and 1:17, with a third construction at 1:9, which is the signature of a passage worked through rather than a phrase remembered. Below any quotation threshold; catalogued as an allusion.

1:17.text: And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.

provenance.other: “the word of God with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the construction ‘spake the word of God with X’ is Acts 4:31's alone. The completing pair is changed: Acts has boldness, Words of Mormon has ‘power and with authority’, and “power and authority” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 9:1 and Luke 20:20.
provenance.significance: Acts 4:31 is the answer to a prayer for boldness under a magistrate's ban, and the boldness is granted along with the Holy Ghost. The Book of Mormon substitutes the Lukan commissioning pair ‘power and authority’, which in Luke 9:1 is what Jesus gives the Twelve when he sends them out. The substitution converts a spontaneous outpouring into a delegated office — which is what the sentence needs, since these prophets are working with the king rather than against a council, and since the next clause has them using sharpness on the strength of that authority.

1:17.note: ‘They did speak the word of God, with power and with authority.’ The frame is Acts 4:31's and is a KJV singleton; the filling is Luke's. Held at moderate rather than high because the frame is four common words and the distinctive word of the source, ‘boldness’, is precisely what the Book of Mormon does not take. What it does take pulls the clause toward the authority-language that the 2 Corinthians 13:10 borrowing in the same verse depends on.

1:17.text: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.

provenance.other: “reign in righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Words of Mormon splits it — ‘reign over his people in righteousness’ — so the contiguous phrase is not reproduced, which is why this is recorded as an echo.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 32:1 is the KJV's one sentence about a righteous king as such, and its second clause pairs the king with subordinate rulers who rule in judgment. Words of Mormon 1:17 supplies both terms: Benjamin reigns in righteousness, and there are many holy men in the land who speak with power and authority. The chapter is introducing the king whose speech occupies the next four chapters of Mosiah, and it introduces him in the words of the one Isaiah verse that defines the office he is about to fill. Isaiah 32 goes on to a spirit poured from on high and to peace as the effect of righteousness; Words of Mormon 1:18 ends on peace established in the land.

1:17.note: ‘King Benjamin was a holy man, and he did reign over his people in righteousness.’ The borrowing is a split KJV singleton and a matching two-part structure — righteous king, righteous subordinates — which is more than the wording alone would support and less than a demonstration. Recorded because of where it stands: this is the sentence that hands the Book of Mormon over to King Benjamin, and Isaiah 32:1 is the verse the King James Bible reserves for exactly that figure. ‘An holy man’ is itself a KJV singleton, at 2 Kings 4:9, but it is used there of Elisha and cannot be pressed here.

1:18.text: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

provenance.other: “with all thy might” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 6:5. The New Testament quotations of the Shema read otherwise: “with all thy strength” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 12:30 and Luke 10:27. `tools/mediation-check.py` on Deuteronomy 6:5 against Mark 12:30 returns one decisive point, and it favours Deuteronomy: the Book of Mormon has ‘might’, not ‘strength’.
provenance.significance: The mediation test is the finding here. Every element of the Shema the Book of Mormon reproduces is in the Old Testament's KJV form and not the Gospels', at the one word where the two differ — which matters because this book's borrowings run heavily to the New Testament, and this chapter alone draws on Matthew or Mark, 2 Peter, Acts, Philippians, Revelation and 2 Corinthians. The verse also does something to its source. Deuteronomy 6:5 commands love of God with all one's might and soul; Words of Mormon 1:18 spends might and soul on the labour of governing a nation back into peace, so the great commandment is redescribed as administrative exhaustion. The prophets and the king labour, and the result is peace in the land.

1:18.note: ‘By laboring with all the might of his body and the faculty of his whole soul.’ The Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy's two distinctive terms, might and soul, each with ‘all’ and ‘whole’, and it has ‘might’ rather than the ‘strength’ that Mark 12:30 and Luke 10:27 read at the same point of the same sentence — so this is the Old Testament KJV, not the Gospels'. ‘Faculty’ occurs in no KJV verse and is the writer's own word. 1830's ‘wherefore … wherefore’ doubling in this verse was tidied in 1920 and has no bearing on the source.
